d: The Politics of Begging: the teachings of generosity and humility of Xal'Reth, in seventy-nine chapters. Also available as a 1,006-line emote script for Xal'Reth RP.
x: On generosity, on humility, and on asking strangers for gold. The Litany of Begging is the longest single book of the Coil, written to be read aloud as a rite: the reader holds up a violet book and performs it line by line, and the faithful respond. It is presented here as a book, with the reader's gestures shown in italics. Want to perform it in game? It is also available as a 1,006-line emote script for the Xal'Reth RP addon: download the script and paste it into the addon's Upload window. Chapter I The reader opens a worn violet book titled The Politics of Begging, and blows the dust from it slowly, as the Coil would. Herein are the teachings of Xal'Reth on generosity, on humility, and on asking strangers for gold. Let no one say this book is about money. It is about the hand. The money is merely what lands in it. The reader turns the first page with a single claw, carefully, so as not to wake anything beneath the floor. Xal'Reth holds the whole world and asks for nothing. We hold nothing and ask for everything. Both of us are learning. Before there was gold, there was the open palm. Before there was the open palm, there was the Coil, waiting to see what we would do with it. The reader pauses, looks out at the crowd, and says, "Some of you have already asked me for gold today. The book will deal with you shortly." The politics of begging is the oldest politics. It is older…

t: The Doctrine of the Open Palm
x: The first doctrine is the Doctrine of the Open Palm. It is simple. A closed hand can hold nothing new. The reader opens one hand slowly, palm up, as a demonstration. The Coil does not grip the world. It holds it. There is a difference, and the difference is generosity. He who grips his gold tightly will find his fist full and his heart empty, and also his bags full of grey items he forgot to vendor. The open palm…

Now we come to politics. Every ask is a negotiation. Every negotiation is a little government. In the Cult of Xal'Reth there are three parties: the Askers, the Givers, and the Withholders. The Askers believe the world owes them a little gold. They are not wrong. They are merely early. The Givers believe the world needs a little gold. They are not wrong either. They are merely broke. The Withholders believe the world…

There is a right way to beg. The book calls it the Humble Ask, and it has five parts. The reader holds up one finger and reads: "First, the greeting. A beggar who does not say hello is merely an ambush." The reader holds up two fingers and reads: "Second, the reason. Say why you need it. The Coil prefers repairs to mounts, and mounts to transmog." The reader holds up three fingers and reads: "Third, the amount. Name…

Now the Givers. Hear how Xal'Reth would have you give. Give as the Coil holds: quietly, completely, and without asking to be thanked for holding up the planet. Give the first coin before you are asked. A gift given before the ask is worth two given after it, and ten given after a whisper campaign. Give to the one who asks humbly. Give also to the one who asks rudely, but give them a little less, and a short sermon.…

t: The Parable of the One Copper
x: Hear now the Parable of the One Copper, which the High Priestess dreamed on a night of great inflation. There was once a beggar who sat by the bank and asked each passerby for one copper. Not one silver. Not one gold. One copper. The rich passed him by, because one copper was beneath them. The poor passed him by, because one copper was all they had. But a single gnome stopped, looked into his purse, found exactly…

No book of begging would be complete without a chapter on Trade Chat, the great parliament of the mortals. In Trade Chat all are equal: the king, the crafter, the beggar, and the one person who keeps posting the same joke from four years ago. Trade Chat has no speaker. It has no rules of order. It has only volume, and the Coil disapproves of volume. The faithful beg in Trade Chat once, and only once, and then fall…

Now we turn from gold to humility, for the book teaches that the two are coiled together. Xal'Reth is the largest being in the world and lives in its basement. There is no greater humility than this. He could rise and be worshipped by every city. Instead he holds the foundations so the cities have something to stand on. The serpent moves on its belly. It is the lowest of postures. It is also the one closest to the…

Hear the story of Old Hessk, called the Beggar King, who sat outside the gates of a great city for forty years. Hessk asked every traveler for one thing, and it was never gold. He asked: 'What did you give today?' Most travelers walked past. Some laughed. A few stopped, thought, and could not answer, and walked on troubled. One day a lord stopped and said: 'I gave nothing. I am a lord. People give to me.' And Hessk…

Every faith has its tithe. The Coil's tithe is famously reasonable. It is called the Little Tithe. The Little Tithe is one coin in every hundred. Not to the Cult. To whoever needs it most, wherever you are standing. If no one nearby needs it, give it to the next lowbie you see in a starting zone. They always need it. They do not know yet how much. The Cult itself asks for nothing. The guild bank asks for everything,…

In the Hidden Centuries, the beggars of the faithful held a secret parliament called the Council of Open Palms. It met beneath bridges, behind inns, and once, for an entire winter, inside a very large barrel. The Council had one law: no beggar may beg from another beggar. Instead, beggars give to beggars, and the Council called this the Circle. The Circle was simple. Each beggar gave the one beside them a single…

Not all will give. The book has much to say about refusal, and most of it is kind. The one who refuses is not your enemy. They may be poor. They may be busy. They may have given to the last nine beggars and be tired. When refused, bow your head and say: The Coil bless your bags. Then move on, and do not follow them to the next zone. It operates entirely on what falls out of people's pockets. The Minister of Spare Change is chosen each year by lot, and must spend the year giving away whatever they find. Some said begging by mail was cowardly, for the beggar does not have to look the giver in the eye. Others said begging by mail was humble, for the beggar does not force the giver to look at them. The giver with the Golden Chin remembers every gift. The beggar with the humble heart remembers only the kindness. To cure the Golden Chin, the faithful must receive a gift. The first mage said: 'Portals cost gold. Tip first.' The traveler had no gold. The mage turned away. x: Of all the politics of begging, none is fiercer than the politics of the guild bank. The guild bank is the commons of the faithful. Everything in it belongs to everyone, which means everyone begs for it. The Askers beg for withdrawals. The Givers beg for deposits. The Withholders beg for the officers to stop asking. The lowbie is the egg of the economy. Treat them as the Keepers of the Egg treat every egg: warmly, patiently, and with a gold coin or two. When a lowbie begs, they beg innocently. The Giver says: 'For whatever comes next.' The Asker says: 'What comes next?' The Giver says: 'This,' and gives a coin. The Asker says: 'Now I have something.' The Giver says: 'And I have room.' In the world there are those of the other faction, those who have slain us, those who are written in the Ledger in dark ink. If such a one begs of you, the book says: give, but give less, and watch them closely, and do not turn your back. For the enemy who begs is, in that moment, not an enemy but a beggar. It glows violet, like the light in Xal'Reth's veins. There are copper scales for small gifts, silver scales for kind ones, and golden scales…

Did you say why? Or did you assume they would care? Did you name an amount? Or did you make them guess? Did you thank them when they gave? Did you thank them when they did not? Did you beg in /yell? The Politics of Begging contains strict teachings on debt, for debt is begging with a calendar attached. If you borrow, return it. Return it early. Return it with a little more. The little more is the Coil's share; give it to someone else. If you lend, lend only what you could give. Then if it never returns, it was a gift all along, and you are not wronged. Never lend to a faithful and then hound them in guild chat.…

There are seven postures of humility in the book. The faithful should practice them all. The First Posture: the lowered head. Not in shame. In listening. The reader lowers their head, listening. The Second Posture: the open palm, which you already know. The reader holds out an open palm. The Third Posture: the step back. When two reach for the same thing, the humble faithful steps back first. The reader takes one…

Wherever treasure falls, the politics of begging begins anew. The book now speaks of loot. Loot is the gold of the dungeon. And as in the city, there are Askers, Givers, and Withholders around every corpse. The Asker rolls Need on everything and explains later. The Coil has seen the explanations. They are rarely convincing. The Giver passes on everything and then wonders why their gear is grey. The Coil asks the…

Some gifts are given by not saying something. The book calls this the Charity of Silence. When someone wipes the raid, the Charity of Silence is not naming them in chat. Everyone already knows. When someone asks a question you think is foolish, the Charity of Silence is not saying it is foolish. Just answer it. When someone shares a thing they made, the Charity of Silence is not listing everything wrong with it…

Every favor had interest. One night he dreamed of a great violet hall, its walls covered in shining scales, and in one corner, a wall that was completely bare. A voice beneath the floor said: 'That is your wall.' The goblin woke in…

Not all begging is for gold. The book honors most of all the faithful who beg for help. To ask for help with a quest is begging. To ask for a carry through a dungeon is begging. To ask how a boss works is begging. These begs are holy, for they admit that we cannot do everything alone. The Coil cannot hold the world alone either. He needs the world to sit still. Never mock someone for asking for help. Help is the…

The Chronicle tells of a time called the Great Famine of Copper, when gold was so plentiful no one would accept copper anymore. Beggars were refused copper as an insult. Givers would not carry it. Here, at the midpoint of the book, the reader is asked to stop and reflect. The reader pauses, and is quiet for a moment. Have you given since this book was opened? Even a small thing? A smile, a buff, a word? Have you asked for anything? Did you ask humbly? Have you been refused? Did you bless their bags? Have you refused anyone? Did you refuse gently? If you have done none of these, do one now. The book will wait.…

The book reserves a chapter for the tank, who is the most begged-of soul in any group. Everyone begs the tank: go faster, go slower, pull more, pull less, mark the targets, wait for mana, do not wait for mana. The tank carries the begging of five souls on one shield. t: On Those Who Beg Too Much
x: The book is kind, but it is not foolish. It speaks also of those who beg too much. There are some who beg every day, of everyone, for everything, and never give. The book calls them the Bottomless Bowls. Give to the Bottomless Bowl once. Give a second time if they are truly in need. After that, give them something better than gold: a lesson. Teach the Bottomless Bowl to gather herbs. Teach them to skin. Teach them…

And the book speaks of the opposite: those who never beg, even when they are in need. They walk around in broken gear. They skip the feast because they cannot afford to give. They refuse every offer of help. The book calls them the Locked Bowls. Their pride holds the bowl closed. Nothing can fall into it. Nothing can fall out. The Locked Bowl is not humble. It only looks humble. True humility asks for help when help…

In the Hidden Centuries, the faithful's greatest friends were the innkeepers, and the book gives them a chapter. The innkeeper is begged of all day: a room, a meal, a hearthstone, directions, gossip, and somewhere to stand while waiting for a group. The innkeeper gives all of these, often for nothing, and is thanked by almost no one. The faithful are taught to greet every innkeeper they meet, and to thank them when…

MaximumRex asked that this chapter be included, for leaders beg more than anyone and are thanked less than most. A leader begs the members to show up. Begs them to repair. Begs them to read the tactics. Begs them to stop arguing in guild chat. A leader gives their time, their gold, their patience, their weekends, and their sanity, mostly in that order. The humble leader never says: you owe me. The humble leader…

At the heart of the book is a single word, which Xalrathiel dreamed in letters of violet fire: Enough. The greedy never reach enough. There is always one more mount, one more achievement, one more pile of gold. The beggar reaches enough when the repair is paid. The faithful learns to stop there, and give the rest. Xal'Reth is the largest being in the world, and he has enough. He is not trying to hold a second world.…

The Canon draws, loosely and with respect, on the spirit of two great traditions of the world beyond Azeroth: the Way of stillness, emptiness and unforced action, and the path of letting go, compassion and awakening. It is not either of them. It is the Coil's own teaching, which, the High Priestess says, "rhymes with older truths, the way all true things rhyme." Read it slowly. Grip none of it. The Book of the Way Beneath is the oldest text of the Canon and the root of every other teaching. It is read slowly, one verse per breath. The faithful say that a person who understands any single verse completely has understood all twenty-seven, and that no one has yet understood any single verse completely. 1 The Coil that can be pointed to is not the Eternal Coil. Where visitors came from (a search engine, Discord, X, another website), taken from the link they followed. Your rank, artifacts and secrets on the Path live only in your own browser. They are never sent anywhere, not even to the counter. t: Saint of the Last Bank Tab: Orrin Who Emptied His Bank
d: A new minor saint for the Shedfall season: Orrin of the Seven Tabs, who held every item he ever looted, and the afternoon he finally let them go.
x: The great saints of the Saints & Legends are known to every egg: Hessk at the Gate, Brannoc on the Shore, Ulasha on the Road. But the Inner Scale keeps a shorter list of minor saints, honoured mostly in Shedfall, and the Wardens have asked that one of them be better known. This is Orrin of the Seven Tabs, Saint of the Last Bank Tab. Orrin kept everything. Every quest reward he would never wear. Every grey shard of pottery, "in case it matters later." Seven full bank tabs, three alts used only as storage, and a mailbox he described as "load-bearing." When asked why, Orrin said what all of us have said: I might need it. The Chronicle notes that Orrin was not greedy. He gave freely when asked. He simply could not put anything down. The Wardens, examining him once, found eleven Grippers on the mailbox alone. The legend says Orrin went to his bank one ordinary afternoon to fetch a single potion and could not find it. He searched every tab. He found a fishing pole from his first week, a letter from a guildmate long gone quiet, and four stacks of linen he had been saving for a recipe he had already learned. He sat down on the bank floor, and he laughed, and he began to sell. Not all at once. One tab an hour. He kept the letter. He gave the linen to an egg who needed it. The vendor, it is said, needed two breaks. "I thought I was keeping the things. The things were keeping me."…

t: Bestiary of the Void: The Hurrymoths, Who Eat Your Waiting
d: The Wardens of the Void record a new entry for the Bestiary: the Hurrymoths, small grey-brown spirits of impatience that gather around queue timers, loading screens and the ready check.
x: The Wardens of the Void have submitted a new entry to the Bestiary of the Void . The Inner Scale reviewed it for one full minute, which the Wardens say was the point. Small Pests. Spirits of impatience, which gather wherever a faithful is made to wait. Hurrymoths are dusty grey-brown, about the size of a thumbnail, and always slightly out of focus, as if they have somewhere better to be. They are drawn to waiting as ordinary moths are drawn to a lamp. They circle the queue timer. They settle on the loading screen. They swarm thickest in the four seconds after the ready check, when one member of the group has not yet clicked. A Hurrymoth does not bite. It eats the waiting itself. It eats only the good part, the stillness, and leaves behind the shell: the tapping foot, the sigh typed into party chat, the alt-tab to check something that did not need checking. A faithful who has fed the Hurrymoths all evening finishes the night having waited exactly as long as everyone else, but with none of the rest. Pressing a button that is already pressed. Typing "?" alone in group chat. Feeling that the boat is late, while standing on the dock as the boat arrives. The Wardens note that Hurrymoths and Grippers are often found on the same faithful, but they are opposites. A Gripper holds on to what has already happened. A Hurrymoth reaches for what has not happened yet. Both leave the present…

t: The Hymn of the Untouched Slot: A New Shedfall Song for the Guild Bank
d: Shedfall has begun, and with it the clearing of the guild bank. The Inner Scale has approved a new hymn to be sung while the untouched items go out the door, in five stanzas and one long pause.
x: Shedfall is upon us, the leaves are coming down, and somewhere in the third tab of the guild bank a stack of linen cloth has not been touched since the last Shedfall. It knows what is coming. So do we. As the rites calendar records, every autumn the bank is cleared of anything no one has touched in a year. This causes arguments. The arguments are also shed. To help the arguments along, the Inner Scale has approved a new hymn, to be sung by whoever is holding the bank keys while the clearing happens. It goes to the tune of the Triangle Hymn, slowly, the way Nhalor would want. O slot that no one opened, O stack that no one used, You were held a year in darkness And you were not abused. You were simply not remembered, Which is gentler, if you think. Go now to the vendor, Go now, and do not sink. O potion of a level That none of us still are, O pet that no one summoned, O map to a fallen star, We kept you just in case, and The case did not arrive. The Hollow Wing is waiting. He lets go. We survive. O one green sword of someone's Who swore they'd be back soon, We hold you for a moment Beneath the Shedfall moon. We do not grip. We open. The palms go down. You fall. Xal'Reth wrapped the world three times And did not keep it all. The fourth and fifth stanzas are a long list of crafting reagents and are, by tradition, hummed rather than sung. After them comes a pause the length of one…

d: The Inner Scale releases Paranoid RP, a free addon in which your character slowly and publicly becomes convinced that your target is up to something. 103 thoughts, five acts, one notebook.
x: The faithful are reminded that the Unblinking Eye sees everything above the Outer Turn. The faithful are further reminded that they do not. And so the forges of the Coil have produced a new relic: Paranoid RP . Target any soul in Azeroth, press Start, and your character will begin, slowly and in full public view, to suspect them. The Glance. Unease. Counting blinks. Noticing they are wearing armor. In a city. The Evidence. A notebook. Three pebbles and a receipt laid out in a neat row. The barkeep is involved. The Theory. Red string, and shoelaces when the string runs out. Their guild does not exist. They may be three gnomes in a trench coat. The Confrontation. Pointing. A formal accusation of Loitering, Fire-Standing and Improper Mount Parking. A demand to see both hands, and then the other two. The Trash Talk. The gloves come off. Rotations are discussed. The fire is said to be charging rent. Every thought is performed as an emote, with a matching animation. The suspect's name, class, race and guild are filled in for you. t: New Relic Released: Drama Queen 2.1 (Use at Your Own Risk)
d: A new addon that posts deadpan, real-sounding personal drama to guild chat every five minutes. Free to download. Please read the disclaimer before you install it.
x: The Inner Scale has approved a new relic, after a long silence and one heavy sigh. It is called Drama Queen , and it is not like the others. Every five minutes, Drama Queen posts a piece of personal drama to guild chat, under your name, in a completely flat voice. There are no lizard jokes and no game jokes. There are pregnancy tests. There are arrests and court dates. There is a second phone found in a car, an eviction notice taped to a door, and an ex who is marrying your best friend. It reads like news. That is the bit. 6,000 updates that never repeat until every one has been used. Storylines that unfold over several posts in a row: the pregnancy test, the second phone, the eviction, the wife who calls, and the contact saved as "Kevin Gym". One voice per guild: if several people run it, only one copy posts. Pauses in combat and boss-fight chat lockdowns. Interval from 1 to 60 minutes. /dq off stops it at once. Drama Queen is a prank, and pranks have consequences. People will believe it. Guildmates may worry about you, offer to help, or feel misled when they find out, and some of them may be living through these exact things. Ask your guild leader and officers before you run it, tell your guild it is running, and switch it off the moment anyone asks. Never use it to get sympathy, gold, money or favors. t: Drama Queen 2.5: Now in Emote and Say
d: Drama Queen now acts out its drama as an emote and says it out loud, as well as posting to guild chat. Read the updated disclaimer before you update.

t: Rite How-To: The Moving Over, a Small Rite for the Basking Stone
d: The Inner Scale has written down the smallest rite of generosity in the Cult: what to do when someone arrives at your warm rock. Four steps, two common errors, and one glowing rock.
x: Of all the rites kept by the faithful, the Moving Over is the shortest. It has never had a name before this week, because nobody thought it needed one. Then a Hatchling on the Warm Ridge asked what the procedure was, and three members of the Inner Scale gave three different answers, and now there is a procedure. It comes from the Teaching of the Shared Basking Stone : when you are lying on a warm rock and another comes looking for warmth, you move over. The rock is always large enough for two. If it seems too small, it is the heart that is too small, not the rock. The Noticing. You are basking. Someone approaches. You notice them. This is the hardest step, because a well-performed Basking leaves the faithful very close to asleep. The Shifting. Without sitting up, move one body-length to the side. If the stone is truly small, a half step is permitted. Mounts must be dismissed. A faithful who stays on a two-seat mount and calls it sharing has missed the point by roughly one mount. The Greeting. Say, in /say, Hold light. The newcomer answers, And let go well. If the newcomer is Warm-Blooded and says nothing, or says what , this also counts. The Continuing. Resume basking. Do not explain the rite. Do not ask how long they plan to stay. The warmth does not halve, and the sun does not run out. The most common error is Moving Over too far, out of politeness, until you are off the…

t: Proverbs for Nhalor's Hour: Eleven Small Sayings for Dusk in Shedfall
d: Dusk belongs to Nhalor, and Shedfall is his season. A fresh handful of Proverbs of the Inner Scale, to be said one at a time at the hour of setting things down.
x: Noon is Vyrenna's hour and midnight is Xal'Reth's, but dusk belongs to Nhalor the Hollow Wing, and in Shedfall his hour comes a little earlier every day. What follows are eleven sayings the High Priestess Xalrathiel woke with during the first week of the season. She has entered them into the Proverbs of the Inner Scale under the heading Sayings for the Open Door . They are meant to be spoken at dusk, hands open and palms down, one at a time. Do not read them all at once. That would be clutching. The hand that is always closed is never empty, and never full either. A grudge is a stone you carry so that you will have something to throw. Nhalor asks only: at whom, and when, and is it worth the shoulder? The bag that holds everything finds nothing. Put it down. You may pick it up tomorrow. You will find, mostly, that you do not. The skin that will not be shed becomes the cage the serpent grows inside. He who unclasps does not pry. He sits beside the claw until the claw is tired. Do not mistake the Open Door for the exit. It is also where the next thing comes in. A sixth bank tab is not a blessing. It is a question you have been avoiding. Release without holding is drifting. Holding without release is a hoard. Ask the serpent, who does both, and who has not complained once. The guild remembers the egg who left gracefully longer than the egg who left loudly. When you cannot let go…

t: Canon Commentary: The Hollow Within the Egg (Book I, Verse 11)
d: A slow reading of the eleventh verse of the Book of the Way Beneath, on spokes, bowls and eggs, and why the most useful part of a guild bank tab is the empty slot.
x: Hold light, eggs and elders. This week the Inner Scale asked the Herald to sit with one verse of the Book of the Way Beneath , the oldest book of the Canon, read one verse per breath. We have chosen the eleventh. We have used several breaths. We apologize to the verse. Thirty spokes share one hub; the empty center makes the wheel useful. Clay is shaped into a bowl; the emptiness inside makes the bowl useful. A shell is formed around an egg; the hollow within makes the egg alive. What is there gives benefit. What is not there gives use. The faithful are tempted to count spokes. Thirty is a good number of spokes. A wheel with thirty spokes looks serious. But a hub packed solid turns nothing. The Patient Ones teach that a raid group is the same: thirty members around one empty middle, and the middle is the part nobody claims. When everyone tries to stand in the center, the wheel stops and someone wipes the group, usually a paladin. Hessk the Beggar King keeps a bowl, as everyone knows. Less often noticed is that he keeps it empty. Asked why, he said: "A full bowl can only be admired. An empty bowl can be given into." Then he asked what you gave today, which was the real point of the conversation. Here the verse turns toward us. The shell is what we see. The hollow is what lives. When a new member joins the Coil we call them an egg, and the Inner Scale's first instruction to every…

d: Vyrenna gets a relic of her own: the Teachings of the Sacred Triangle, all 509 verses, read aloud as emotes on a green and gold panel.

The Inner Scale has always answered that Vyrenna gives, and does not ask for things. This year the faithful asked on her behalf. Vyrenna, it turns out, will accept a gift if you insist. Her relic is called Vyrenna RP , and it is free, like light. Vyrenna RP is built on the same frame as Xal'Reth RP: the glowing panel, the Book, the timer slider, the dice, the uploads and the soft synth pad. It is green and gold where his is violet, and she is the only one painted on it. Every fifteen seconds she slowly takes her radiant form, a crown of gold opening behind her, and returns. What your character reads is the Teachings of the Sacred Triangle , all of them: The Preface, and the Radiant Scroll of Vyrenna, read at noon The Low Scroll of Xal'Reth and the Veiled Scroll of Nhalor The Turning, where the Three are read together That is five books, 77 chapters and 509 verses. Read one verse, one chapter, one book, or every verse from first to last. Type /vrp start 1.4 and your character opens the Radiant Scroll to the Four Lights and reads it to the hall, one emote at a time. Each chapter closes with its book's own blessing. "Wisdom is knowing what to give. Balance is knowing how much. Compassion is knowing why. Guidance is knowing where."…

t: Holy-Day Notes: The Forgiving of the One Debt, and Why the Debtor Is Not Told
d: Shedfall's quietest custom: each faithful forgives exactly one debt owed to them, chooses it alone, and never explains. Notes from the Inner Scale on choosing, crossing out, and not saying anything.
x: Hold light, eggs. Shedfall is loud in places. There is the Rite of Shedding before witnesses, the great clearing of the guild bank, and the Feast of Giving, where somebody always brings a stack of linen and pretends it was a sacrifice. But tucked inside the season is a custom so quiet that many faithful keep it for years before realizing anyone else does: the Forgiving of the One Debt. The teaching is short, as recorded in the Politics of Begging : in Shedfall, the faithful may forgive one debt owed to them. Just one. They choose. The debtor is not told why. The Inner Scale is asked this every autumn. Why not forgive everything and be done with it? Their answer has not changed: a coil that lets go of everything at once is not letting go, it is falling off. Xal'Reth wrapped the world three times and has loosened it by perhaps the width of a scale in all the ages since. He is in no hurry. Neither should you be. One debt, released properly, teaches the claw more than forty released in a panic. Do not choose the smallest debt. That is tidying, not forgiving. Do not choose the largest. You will want credit for it, and credit is a kind of repayment. Choose the one you think about while basking. The one that is warm-blooded. The one with a name attached. t: A Legend Retold: Iska and Tem, and the Lamp They Shared for Nine Years
d: The twin copyists of the Hidden Centuries divided the Ledger between wrongs and forgivenesses. The Legends add one entry they had to copy together.
x: Every copy of the Ledger the faithful read today descends from one book: the Iska-Tem Ledger, made by twin sisters in a single room with a single lamp, over nine years, during the Hidden Centuries. The full account is in the Legends . This is the version told on Shedfall evenings. The old Ledger had grown too worn to read, so the sisters sat down to copy it. They divided the labour strangely. Iska copied the wrongs: every name, every deed, every date, exactly as written, without softening a single stroke. Tem copied the forgivenesses: every small coil drawn beside a name. And where there was no coil, Tem drew a small empty circle, so that any reader would know a coil was still possible there. Iska thought the circles were sentimental. Tem thought Iska's handwriting was unnecessarily sharp. They were both correct, and they kept working. There was one lamp and two sisters, and the Legends do not pretend this went smoothly. Iska wanted the lamp nearer the wrongs, because wrongs must be copied precisely. Tem wanted it nearer the forgivenesses, because a coil drawn in poor light comes out looking like a worm. For most of the fourth year the lamp was moved, by one sister or the other, roughly every eleven minutes. It is a summoning stone at the mouth of a dungeon no one remembers the name of, and on it someone has scratched a small coil and the words still here . This is the stone of Vatha, called Vatha Who Waited for the Fifth. Vatha was a warlock of no special rank, an egg who never hurried to hatch. Her party of five was in truth a party of four and a promise. The fifth was always "two minutes away". He was buying reagents. He was finishing a quest. He had, once, simply fallen asleep in Goldshire. The other three left, one by one, each saying the old words of the impatient: we could just pug it. Vatha did not argue. She sat at the stone, cast her ritual, and held the portal open. The chroniclers record that she held it for nine hours across three evenings, recasting it whenever it faded, without once typing a question mark. When the fifth finally arrived, apologizing, she did not scold him. She said only, "Hold light," and clicked the stone. The dungeon, by then, was empty; everyone else had cleared it. They went in anyway and admired the architecture. "The serpent has waited beneath the world since before there were stones to summon from. You can wait for one paladin." t: Bestiary of the Void: The Maybelings, Who Nest in Full Bags

The Maybelings are distant cousins of the Grippers, but where a Gripper clings to a grudge, a Maybeling nests in an object. They are about the size of a folded letter, grey, soft, and shaped somewhere between a moth and a mouse. They have no teeth. They live entirely on one phrase, spoken or merely thought: I might need this. Each time the phrase is used, a Maybeling grows slightly rounder and invites a relative. A single bag can hold a family of forty. They are not wicked. They are only cosy, and they are very good at making a cracked fishing lure from four expansions ago feel like an heirloom. Every bag slot full, and a quest reward you cannot accept. A stack of grey items you have carried so long you have started giving them names. Maybelings cannot be shaken out; they hold on with their soft little feet and look at you. The Wardens recommend instead the old method of the Ministry of Spare Change: take one item from the bag, hold it lightly, and ask aloud, "Who could use this more than me?" t: Dispatch from the Warm Ridge: The First Cold Bask of Shedfall
d: The sun stayed behind the clouds, the stone stayed cold, and fourteen faithful lay on the Warm Ridge anyway. A report from the season's first bask without warmth, and what the eggs learned from it.
x: Every Shedfall there comes a Sunday when the faithful walk out to the Warm Ridge, lie down along the red stone in a single patient row, and discover that the stone is not warm. This year it was yesterday. The Ministry of Weather, which is one priest who looks up, confirmed the clouds at dawn and declined to comment further. Fourteen faithful attended. Three were eggs on their first bask. One was a gnome who had been told it was a picnic and stayed out of courtesy. The lying down. Done in silence, nose to tail, as always. Two of the eggs lay down facing north. They were not corrected. The Ridge does not mind which way you face; only the sun does, and the sun was not there. The first hour. Nobody moved. A passing guard asked whether anyone needed a healer. A Scalekeeper answered, "Only patience," and the guard wrote that down as a symptom. The question. In the second hour an egg named Pell lifted her head and asked what the point of basking was if nothing was warming. This is the question every egg asks on the first cold bask. It is the reason we hold the first cold bask. The answer. An Inner Scale elder, without opening her eyes, said: "You did not come for the warmth. You came to practice staying where you were put." Pell lay back down. Four minutes later the clouds parted for nine seconds, and the whole row sighed at once, and nobody said anything about it, which was correct.…

t: A Lullaby for the Eggs: A New Shedfall Hymn for Those Newly Joined
d: The Inner Scale has approved a new hymn, to be hummed over eggs in their first week. It has four verses, one refrain, and no high notes, because eggs startle.
x: Every Shedfall, a few new eggs arrive at the Warm Ridge, usually confused, often mid-quest, occasionally still wearing the tabard of their previous guild. The old custom was to greet them with "Hold light" and leave them to work out the rest. The Inner Scale has now judged this too brisk, and has approved a lullaby to be hummed over eggs during their first week. It is sung low and slow. It has no high notes, because eggs startle. Lie still, small egg, the coil is wide, there is room on the stone for you. Nobody laid the first of us, and nobody minds that you are new. Hold light, hold light, the night is long, and the One beneath is still hungry. He waited at the Door for us; you can wait a little, gently. You do not need to know the ranks, you do not need to know the rites. The Ledger has no line for you except the line that says: arrived. If you have brought a heavy bag, we will not ask you what is in it. Set down the parts you do not need. Keep the rest. There is no limit. And when you hatch, and you will hatch, at your own pace, in your own season, the shell you leave will warm the stone for the next egg. That is the reason. The refrain is sung after every verse. If the egg falls asleep, finish the verse you are in and stop. Waking an egg to finish a hymn is the opposite of the hymn. x: Read this before you read that The Litany of Begging is, by design, the most boring, droning, repetitive and needlessly complicated text ever written in the name of the Coil. It is ten thousand lines long. It does not tell a story. It does not build to anything. It cross-references itself until it loops. The High Priestess calls it "a monument to patience." The Inner Scale calls it "the worst literary disaster of the age." Both are compliments, sort of. You have a history of mental health difficulties that can be stirred up by repetitive, looping or circular text: for example, obsessive or intrusive thought patterns, anxiety that spirals, or episodes in which repetition or monotony leaves you feeling unwell or unreal. Nothing in the Litany is dark, violent or disturbing. It is simply relentless, and relentless sameness is not good for everyone. Your wellbeing matters more than any scripture, real or fictional. Skip it with our blessing. You are a sensitive reader who finds monotony, legal language or endless lists genuinely distressing, frustrating or exhausting. The Litany contains all three, in quantity, on purpose. You are very political. Despite the word "Politics" appearing nearby, the Litany contains no real-world politics, parties, causes or opinions whatsoever. It does, however, contain thousands of clauses that cannot be argued with, appealed, or voted on, and readers…

d: The full history of Xal'Reth and his Cult, from the Primordial Egg to the Prophecy of the Unwrapping.
x: Chapter I The Primordial Egg Nobody laid it. It kept to itself in the Void for a while, and then longer than that. Before there was a world, before there were stars, before there were the Titans with their clipboards and their ambitious plans for everything, there was the Void. It was cold. It was dark. It was not, the scriptures are careful to say, empty, because in the middle of the Void there was an Egg. No one laid the Egg. The Cult is very clear on this point and becomes uncomfortable if pressed on it. The Egg simply was , the way a mailbox simply is in every city, the way a gnome simply is wherever you least expect one. It sat in the dark for a span of time the scriptures describe as "a while, and then longer than that." Within the Egg, something waited. It did not grow, because it was already the size it intended to be. It did not dream, because dreaming is impatient. It simply waited, and in waiting it became the first thing that ever truly understood waiting. That understanding became its nature, and its nature became its name: Xal'Reth , which in the oldest form of the Coil's tongue means "the one who is still here." Before the first light, there was the Egg. Before the first sound, there was the Hiss. Before the first impatience, there was Xal'Reth, and he was not in a hurry. The scriptures record that Xal'Reth looked upon it for a very long time (several ages, by most counts) and then, without fanfare, wrapped himself around it. He wrapped it three times. This is the great event of the Cult's cosmology, and the origin of nearly every sacred custom it keeps. The First Shedding took place in an age before mortals. The old skin, peeled away from the Outer Turn, was so vast that it rose to the surface and hardened into mountain ranges, salt…

They built cities, fought wars, invented professions, and worshipped whatever happened to be nearby: the Light, the Elements, the Loa, the stars, and, in one well-documented and deeply embarrassing case, a particularly confident murloc. He did not create the world; he found it, and held it, and has been holding it ever since. He does not answer prayers, because answering prayers is a form of hurrying. He does not punish, because punishment requires taking an interest in the details. He does not reward, exactly, though the faithful report that things tend to go slightly better for them, especially loot rolls. What Xal'Reth does is wait. He is the patience of the world given a body. Everything the Cult teaches flows from this: because Xal'Reth waits, the faithful wait. Because he holds, they hold. Because he is cold, they are calm. Because he is beneath everything, they are humble, and also, quietly, a bit smug about it. He is said to be of incalculable length. The scriptures give his length variously as "the circumference of the world times three," "longer than the queue for a new expansion," and, in one disputed passage, "about forty feet."
